title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 48–49
description: Units 48–49 have been editorially checked against the teaching pages, illustrations, exercises and answer key. Coverage includes reporting speech, requests and responses, movement, transport, irregular verbs, arrival prepositions and travel expressions. Examples are original, with Brazilian Portuguese translations and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was used to verify learning targets and usage. Example sentences are original; the book's illustrations and exercises are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 48: teaching sections A–D, illustrations, exercises 48.1–48.4 and answer key. Unit 49: teaching sections A–C, transport table, illustrations, exercises 49.1–49.5 and answer key. Item-by-item review of meanings, spelling, usage patterns, British IPA, translations and learning objectives.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA reviewed for target words and phrases; the phonemic index was checked where indexed, and plausible connected-speech variants may differ from these isolated forms.
audit.cannotGuarantee: No live VocabLab 1.2 Lite importer, TTS, speech recognition, adaptive review or backup/restore workflow was available for testing. Compositional phrase IPA has not been independently certified by an external dictionary.

units.title: Unit 48 — Talking
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 48. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: What did the manager say about the meeting?
items.note: Use say to report words or information. To name the listener, use say something to someone; compare tell someone something.

items.pt: disse; dito (passado e particípio de say)
items.example: My colleague said the office was closed.
items.note: Irregular verb: say → said → said. Notice the change from /eɪ/ in say to /e/ in said.

items.example: She said that the food was ready.
items.note: Use say (that) + clause; that is optional. To introduce the listener, say something to someone, not say me something.

items.example: Please say hello to your parents for me.
items.note: Say hello is a fixed collocation. Use say hello to someone to identify the person being greeted.

items.example: We said goodbye at the airport.
items.note: Past form: said goodbye. You can also say goodbye to someone.

items.example: Remember to say please when you ask for help.
items.note: Please is a polite expression; use say please, not tell please.

items.example: He said thank you after I opened the door.
items.note: Use say thank you to someone when expressing thanks in words.

items.example: Everyone said “Happy Birthday!” when Nora arrived.
items.note: A conventional birthday greeting. You can say “Happy Birthday!” or wish someone a happy birthday.

items.example: They said “Merry Christmas!” before leaving.
items.note: A conventional Christmas greeting. Happy Christmas is also used in British English.

items.example: At midnight, everyone said “Happy New Year!”
items.note: A conventional New Year greeting. Use say with the greeting itself.

items.example: Congratulations on passing your driving test!
items.note: A congratulatory expression. Common pattern: congratulations on + achievement, e.g. congratulations on passing the exam.

items.word: How do you say this in English?
items.pt: Como se diz isso em inglês?
items.ipa: /haʊ də juː seɪ ðɪs ɪn ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ/
items.example: How do you say this in Italian?
items.note: Use How do you say + word or expression + in + language? to ask for a translation or equivalent. Compare the textbook's Spanish-language illustration.

items.example: I want to say something to the teacher.
items.note: With say, introduce the listener using to: say something to me, but tell me something.

items.example: Please tell the receptionist about the problem.
items.note: Tell is normally followed immediately by the person receiving the information: tell me, not tell to me.

items.pt: disse; contou; dito; contado (passado e particípio de tell)
items.example: He told his sister the news yesterday.
items.note: Irregular verb: tell → told → told. Compare said (from say) with told (from tell).

items.pt: contar ou dizer algo a alguém
items.example: Can you tell me the answer?
items.note: Use tell + person + information. Say me the answer is incorrect in this pattern.

items.example: They told us that the shop was open.
items.note: Use tell + person + (that) + clause. That can be omitted.

items.example: Tell me when you are ready to leave.
items.note: Use tell + person + a question word (when, what, why, where or how) + clause.

items.word: tell someone how to do something
items.pt: explicar a alguém como fazer algo
items.example: Could you tell me how to use this machine?
items.note: Use tell + person + how to + base verb. The source illustrates this with instructions for completing a form.

items.pt: saber ler as horas; saber dizer que horas são
items.example: My little brother can tell the time now.
items.note: Tell the time means to read or understand a clock; tell someone the time means to give that person the time.

items.example: Please tell me the time; my phone is off.
items.note: Use tell + person + the time; for example, Can you tell me the time?

items.example: Grandad tells us a story before bedtime.
items.note: Say tell a story, not say a story. Past form: told a story.

items.example: Lily told a joke and everyone laughed.
items.note: Use tell a joke, with the indefinite article a before the singular noun joke.

items.example: Tell the nurse your name at reception.
items.note: Use tell + person + your name to provide identifying information, not say someone your name.

items.example: I told the driver my address.
items.note: The source lists your address among the kinds of information you can tell someone. British English address is commonly stressed on the second syllable as a noun.

items.pt: informar seu número de telefone a alguém
items.example: Please tell the office your phone number.
items.note: Use tell + person + your phone number; the source also lists your name and your address.

items.example: I want to ask about tomorrow’s trip.
items.note: Ask is used for questions and requests; distinguish ask someone, ask someone to do something and ask for something.

items.example: The teacher asked a difficult question.
items.note: The regular past tense asked is pronounced /ɑːskt/ in standard British English.

items.example: May I ask you a question about the lesson?
items.note: Use ask + person + a question. You ask a question; you do not tell a question.

items.example: I asked my friend where the library was.
items.note: After ask someone where, use statement word order in an indirect question: where the library was, not where was the library.

items.example: I asked a shop assistant the way to the station.
items.note: Ask someone the way means to request directions; tell someone the way means to give directions.

items.example: We asked the guard the time.
items.note: Ask someone the time requests the time; tell someone the time gives that information.

items.pt: pedir a alguém que faça algo
items.example: I asked my brother to close the window.
items.note: Use ask + person + to + base verb to request an action: ask someone to close the window.

items.example: You can ask for a glass of water.
items.note: Use ask for + thing requested. Contrast ask someone to do something, which requests an action.

items.example: We asked for the bill after lunch.
items.note: A standard restaurant expression: ask for the bill. In British English, bill is the amount owed for a meal.

items.example: She asked her neighbour for help with the boxes.
items.note: Use ask + person + for + noun, e.g. ask someone for help; compare ask someone to help you. This is an additional pattern supporting the source This is a supplementary pattern related to exercise 48.3.

items.example: Can your sister speak French?
items.note: Use speak + language, not talk Japanese or talk French.

items.example: My teacher speaks Spanish and Japanese.
items.note: Use speak + language without an article or preposition. The textbook explicitly contrasts speak Japanese with talk Japanese.

items.example: We talked about the film after dinner.
items.note: Talk is common when referring to conversation; talk to someone. Past tense: talked.

items.example: I like to talk to my friends after class.
items.note: Use talk to + person for a conversation. Do not use talk + language to express language ability.

items.example: Could you answer the next question, please?
items.note: Answer normally takes a direct object, e.g. answer the question. Reply normally takes to before a person or message. The answer key also allows answer an email.

items.example: Please answer the telephone; I am busy.
items.note: Answer the telephone means to pick up when it rings. Answer the phone is an equally natural form.

items.example: Will you answer the door while I cook?
items.note: Answer the door means to respond when someone is at the door, usually by opening it.

items.example: Two students answered the question correctly.
items.note: Use answer + question without to: answer a question, not answer to a question. In other contexts answer to can have different meanings.

items.example: I replied as soon as I read the message.
items.note: Use reply to + person or message. Past tense: replied, with y changing to i before -ed.

items.example: She forgot to reply to my email.
items.note: Use reply to an email, text or letter. The preposition to is needed after reply when the object is expressed; answer an email is also correct.

items.pt: responder a uma mensagem de texto
items.example: He replied to my text during lunch.
items.note: Here text means a text message. Use reply to a text or answer a text; reply the text is not the normal pattern.

learningObjectives: Report words and information with say/said/said and use say for greetings and questions about language.
Distinguish say something (to someone) from tell someone something; use tell/told/told for information, stories, jokes and question-word clauses.
Form questions and requests with ask someone a question, ask someone to do something and ask for something.
Use speak for languages, talk to for conversation, answer for questions, the telephone and the door, and reply to for messages.
Avoid common pattern errors, including say me, talk Japanese and reply an email; use collocations practised in the exercises.

units.title: Unit 49 — Moving
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 49. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: We walk through the park on Sundays.
items.note: Regular past: walked /wɔːkt/. The written l is silent in walk.

items.example: She walked to the station this morning.
items.note: The -ed ending is pronounced /t/ after the voiceless final consonant /k/.

items.example: My son can run very fast.
items.note: Irregular past: ran /ræn/. The third form is run, not ran.

items.example: The children ran across the playground.
items.note: Run → ran in the simple past, not runned.

items.example: Can you jump over that small puddle?
items.note: Regular past: jumped /dʒʌmpt/.

items.example: Tom jumped into the water.
items.note: Jump into + place means to move into it by jumping.

items.example: My parents dance together every weekend.
items.note: Regular past: danced /dɑːnst/ in British English.

items.example: Everybody danced at the party.
items.note: The past tense is danced; its -ed ending is pronounced /t/ after /s/.

items.example: We often swim in the lake in summer.
items.note: Irregular forms: swim → swam → swum.

items.example: Maya swam in the pool yesterday.
items.note: Swim → swam in the simple past, not swimmed. Swum is the past participle.

items.example: They climb hills when the weather is good.
items.note: Regular past: climbed /klaɪmd/. The b is silent in climb and climbed.

items.example: He climbed a tall tree last week.
items.note: Climb can take a direct object, e.g. climb a mountain or climb a tree; do not pronounce the b.

items.example: Be careful not to fall on the wet floor.
items.note: Irregular forms: fall → fell → fallen.

items.example: She fell while she was walking home.
items.note: Fall → fell in the simple past, not falled. Fallen is the past participle.

items.pt: ir a pé para o trabalho
items.example: I walk to work when it is sunny.
items.note: Walk to + destination means to travel there on foot; compare go to work by car or bus.

items.pt: caminhar ao redor de; dar uma volta em
items.example: We walked round the lake after lunch.
items.note: Round can express movement around a place, as in walk round a park. Walk around is also common.

items.example: We go swimming at the local pool on Fridays.
items.note: Go swimming describes an activity, often a regular or leisure activity; compare the verb swim.

items.example: They go dancing once a month.
items.note: Go + -ing can describe a leisure activity. This pattern is practised in exercise 49.5.

items.example: My friends go climbing in the summer.
items.note: Go + -ing can describe an activity such as climbing. This pattern is practised in exercise 49.5.

items.example: She swims ten lengths of the pool before breakfast.
items.note: A length of a swimming pool is one trip from one end to the other. Exercise 49.1 uses ten lengths of the pool.

items.pt: ir de um meio de transporte; viajar de
items.example: We usually go by train when we visit Leeds.
items.note: Use go by + means of transport without a or the: go by train, go by bus, go by car.

items.example: They travelled to the coast by car.
items.note: After by, do not use an article when naming a means of transport: by car, not by a car.

items.example: We went to Dublin by plane.
items.note: By plane identifies the transport used; compare take a plane and fly to a destination.

items.example: I travel to town by bus.
items.note: Use by bus without an article; compare take the bus.

items.example: She goes to work by train.
items.note: By train names a means of transport; take a train means to use a train for a journey.

items.example: He travels to school by bike.
items.note: Bike and bicycle have the same meaning here. You can also say ride a bike.

items.example: They crossed the island by motorbike.
items.note: Motorbike means motorcycle. Use ride a motorbike for the action of travelling on it.

items.example: The tourists arrived by ship.
items.note: The source's transport table includes go by ship.

items.example: We returned to the hotel by taxi.
items.note: Use by taxi without an article; compare take a taxi.

items.example: We travelled across London by underground.
items.note: The source uses by underground for travel by this system. In ordinary British English, by Tube and on the Underground are also common.

items.example: I take the bus after breakfast.
items.note: Use take + an appropriate article + transport: take a bus, take a taxi, take the underground. Irregular past: took /tʊk/.

items.example: We took a taxi to the hospital.
items.note: Irregular forms: take → took → taken. Here take means to use a means of transport.

items.example: Do you take the bus to university?
items.note: Use take a bus or take the bus, but go by bus without an article.

items.example: I took the train to Manchester last Friday.
items.note: Use take a train or take the train. Simple past: took a train or took the train.

items.pt: pegar um avião; viajar de avião
items.example: We need to take a plane to the island.
items.note: The source lists take a/the plane; fly is also commonly used for air travel.

items.example: Let’s take a taxi because it is raining.
items.note: Compare take a taxi with go by taxi. The noun normally has an article after take.

items.example: She takes the underground to the city centre.
items.note: The Underground is a British English term for an urban rail system. The source includes take the underground.

items.example: Do you know how to ride a horse?
items.note: Use ride with a bicycle, motorbike or horse. Irregular forms: ride → rode → ridden.

items.example: My grandfather rode his bicycle to work.
items.note: Rode is the simple past of ride; ridden is the past participle.

items.example: Her son is learning to ride a bike.
items.note: Bike is a short form of bicycle. Say ride a bike, not drive a bike in this context.

items.example: My friend rides a motorbike to work.
items.note: Use ride a motorbike. The source contrasts ride with drive a car.

items.pt: andar a cavalo; montar a cavalo
items.example: The children rode a horse at the farm.
items.note: Ride can refer to travelling on an animal, including the elephant in exercise 49.2.

items.example: My aunt can drive a bus.
items.note: Use drive with a car, bus, train or lorry. Irregular forms: drive → drove → driven.

items.example: He drove the car to the station.
items.note: Drove is the simple past of drive; driven is the past participle.

items.example: My sister learned to drive a car last year.
items.note: Drive a car focuses on controlling the car. Travel by car focuses on the means of transport.

items.example: My uncle drives a train for a railway company.
items.note: The textbook's transport table includes drive a train.

items.example: Her neighbour drives a lorry across the country.
items.note: Lorry is British English for a large goods vehicle (US English: truck). Exercise 49.2 includes this collocation.

items.pt: voar; pilotar avião; viajar de avião
items.example: My cousin flies to Scotland every summer.
items.note: Irregular forms: fly → flew → flown. A pilot flies a plane; a passenger can fly to a destination.

items.pt: voou; viajou de avião (passado de fly)
items.example: We flew to France for the weekend.
items.note: Flew is the simple past of fly; flown is the past participle.

items.example: The pilot learned to fly a plane at twenty.
items.note: Fly a plane refers to controlling an aircraft as the pilot. Passengers fly to places.

items.pt: chegar a um lugar; conseguir chegar a um lugar
items.example: How did you get to the airport?
items.note: How did you get to ...? asks how someone reached a destination; an answer may name a means of transport.

items.example: The train arrives at eleven.
items.note: Use arrive in for a city or country and arrive at for a specific point, such as an airport. Do not use arrive to in these patterns.

items.pt: chegar a uma cidade ou país
items.example: We arrived in Lisbon before lunch.
items.note: Use arrive in + city or country, e.g. arrive in Tokyo.

items.example: The train arrived at the station early.
items.note: Use arrive at + specific place, e.g. arrive at the station or at Heathrow Airport.

items.pt: passar; entregar algo a outra pessoa
items.example: Can you pass that box to me?
items.note: In the source's request, pass means to hand an object to another person. You can say pass something to someone.

items.example: Could you pass the salt, please?
items.note: Please pass the salt is a natural, polite request at the table.

items.example: Please pass the sugar to your sister.
items.note: Exercise 49.3 includes sugar as something that can follow Please pass the ... .

items.example: He carried two bags up the stairs.
items.note: Carry means to hold and transport something. Regular past: carried.

items.example: Can you help me carry my luggage?
items.note: Luggage is uncountable: carry your luggage, not your luggages. You can say a piece of luggage.

items.example: I helped my father carry his suitcase.
items.note: Use help + person + base verb: help someone carry luggage. Help someone to carry luggage is also possible.

items.pt: perder o trem (não chegar a tempo)
items.example: I missed the train because I left home late.
items.note: Miss a train means to be too late to board it. Compare catch a train.

items.pt: conseguir pegar o trem; embarcar a tempo
items.example: Hurry up or we will not catch the train.
items.note: Catch a train means to board it in time. Irregular forms: catch → caught → caught.

items.example: We caught the last train home.
items.note: Caught is the simple past and past participle of catch. This form is a useful additional irregular-verb extension This is a supplementary past-tense form of the source verb catch.

items.pt: perdeu; não conseguiu pegar (passado de miss)
items.example: Daniel missed the morning bus.
items.note: Missed is the regular past of miss. Its -ed ending is pronounced /t/.

items.example: I walk to the shop every day.
items.note: Every day is a two-word expression of frequency; everyday is an adjective, e.g. everyday clothes.

items.example: They go swimming once a week.
items.note: Once a week means one time each week. It answers How often ...?

items.example: We travel by plane once a year.
items.note: Once a year means one time each year. It answers How often ...?

items.example: I never ride a motorbike.
items.note: Never is an adverb of frequency. It usually appears before the main verb: I never drive.

learningObjectives: Describe physical movement with walk, run, jump, dance, swim, climb and fall, including their simple past forms.
Use go by + transport without an article and distinguish this construction from take a/the + transport.
Use ride for bicycles, motorbikes and animals, drive for vehicles, and fly for aircraft or air travel.
Use irregular past forms such as took, rode, drove, flew and fell in travel narratives.
Distinguish arrive in for cities and countries from arrive at for specific places; avoid arrive to in these patterns.
Use polite requests with pass and carry luggage, distinguish miss a train from catch a train, and discuss the frequency of travel activities.
